Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Digital payment infrastructure is actively used for government revenue collection. The E-levy (Electronic Transaction Levy, introduced May 2022) taxed electronic transactions at 1% and collected GH₵810.5M in H1 2024 and GH₵1.19B in 2023 against a GH₵1.11B target. The GRA's Taxpayers' Portal integrates with Ghana.gov for digital tax payments via mobile money and bank cards. VAT e-invoicing (E-VAT) system is being rolled out. The GRA has deployed a Taxpayer Portal, E-invoicing Portal, and E-VAT Portal. E-levy has since been repealed (2025), but other digital revenue mechanisms remain active.
revision_notes: Original sources (GRA portal, Oxford Business Group, ceditalk) remain live and relevant. E-levy repealed April 2025 (confirmed via EY tax alert and 2026 budget statement), but GRA Taxpayers' Portal continues to enable digital payment of income tax, VAT and other revenue via mobile money/bank card; GRA reported GHS33.7bn collected in Q1 2026, 20% up year-on-year, confirming continued digital revenue collection. Score of 3 (Yes) confirmed with updated 2025-2026 evidence.
revised_comments: Government revenue, including taxes and duties, can be paid digitally via the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) Taxpayers' Portal, which integrates with Ghana.gov for payment by mobile money and bank card. The Electronic Transfer Levy (E-levy) was repealed in April 2025, but other digital revenue channels continue to expand: VAT reforms took effect in 2026 (rate reduced to 20%, registration threshold raised) and GRA reported GHS33.7 billion collected in the first quarter of 2026, 20% higher than the same period in 2025. The GRA operates a Taxpayer Portal, E-invoicing Portal and E-VAT Portal for digital tax administration.

Definition: Whether an official government web portal or mobile application exists where taxpayers can file tax returns and pay taxes online with direct e-payment capability linked to instant payment system.
Comments: Ghana has a fully operational tax portal. The GRA Taxpayers' Portal (taxpayersportal.com) and mobile App were officially launched April 2022. The portal allows online filing of all tax returns, generation of tax bills, and initiation of tax payments via Ghana.gov using Mobile Money, Bank Card, USSD *222# or bank. Tax clearance certificates are now only available through the portal. The GRA has also deployed an e-invoicing system for VAT (E-VAT, being phased in from Oct 2022 through 2024). Ghana Card PIN is used as TIN for individual taxpayers. The portal is mandatory for excise taxpayers and those with annual revenue above GHS5M.
revision_notes: Confirmed the GRA Taxpayers' Portal (taxpayersportal.com) remains operational in 2026, continuing to allow online filing and e-payment of taxes via mobile money, bank card, USSD *222# and bank. GRA's Q1 2026 revenue performance report (April 2026) confirms ongoing digital tax administration. Score of 4 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: Ghana operates a fully functioning tax portal. The Ghana Revenue Authority's Taxpayers' Portal (taxpayersportal.com) and companion mobile app, launched in April 2022, allow taxpayers to file returns and pay taxes online via mobile money, bank card, USSD *222# or bank visit. Tax clearance certificates are issued only through the portal, and the portal is mandatory for excise taxpayers and businesses with annual revenue above GHS5 million. The GRA has also rolled out complementary e-invoicing (E-VAT) and e-invoicing portals to widen digital tax administration.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: B2B digital payments are fully available. GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP) supports corporate payments including payroll, with a per-transaction limit of GH₵50,000 and bank API integration. The Ghana Automated Clearing House (GACH) handles bulk direct credit/debit for businesses. RTGS/GIS handles large-value B2B settlements. GhQR supports B2B merchant payments. The Bank of Ghana's 2023 Annual Report notes GhIPSS Instant Pay is 'widely adopted for both personal transfers and large-scale corporate payments like payroll.' PAPSS also enables B2B cross-border payments for Ghanaian companies.
revision_notes: GhIPSS 2025 industry performance data confirms GIP continues to support high-value corporate/business transactions (GHS1.73 trillion processed in 2025, up 50% year-on-year), consistent with B2B use. Original Bank of Ghana 2023 report language on GIP corporate payroll adoption also verified as still accurate. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed with fresher 2025 data.
revised_comments: Business-to-business digital payments are supported through GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP), which enables corporate payments including payroll and supplier settlements, with bank API integration and a per-transaction limit of GHS50,000. In 2025 GhIPSS processed 530 million transactions worth GHS1.73 trillion, a 50% increase in value year-on-year, reflecting continued growth in high-value institutional and business use of the platform. The Ghana Automated Clearing House (GACH) and RTGS/GIS also support bulk and large-value B2B settlement, while PAPSS enables cross-border B2B payments for Ghanaian firms.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Cross-border payments are partially functional with active development. Ghana's first PAPSS transaction occurred March 2023 (GCB Bank, Ghana Cedi to Nigeria Naira). PAPSS went live in Ghana in 2023, with 19 Ghanaian banks now connected (second only to Nigeria's 22). An Onafriq-PAPSS cross-border pilot launched June 2025 for outbound mobile money transfers, approved by Bank of Ghana for a 6-month evaluation. Inward remittances via GhIPSS Instant Pay platform are active. However, full mobile-money-based intra-African cross-border is still in pilot stage as of 2025, hence 'partially functional' rather than fully functional.
revision_notes: PAPSS network coverage document (June 2026) confirms 16+ Ghanaian banks are live PAPSS participants (including GCB, Ecobank, Stanbic, UBA, Zenith, Prudential, and the Agricultural Development Bank which joined April 2025), with Ghana hosting PAPSS' own headquarters. Cross-border bank transactions are well established. However, the consumer-facing mobile money cross-border pilot with Onafriq remained a pilot as of 2025, and coverage is limited to PAPSS member countries (around 11-15 live), not universal. Score of 4 (Partially functional) confirmed rather than upgraded to Fully functional, given the continuing pilot status of the mass-market mobile money leg.
revised_comments: Cross-border instant payments are partially functional and expanding steadily. Ghana hosts the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) headquarters, launched in Accra in January 2022, and by 2026 more than 15 Ghanaian banks are live PAPSS participants, including GCB, Ecobank, Stanbic, UBA, Zenith and the Agricultural Development Bank (which joined in April 2025), enabling real-time local-currency settlement with other African countries. A consumer-facing mobile-money cross-border pilot with Onafriq launched in mid-2025 under Bank of Ghana supervision. Coverage remains limited to PAPSS member countries and the mobile-money leg is still at pilot stage, so cross-border functionality is best described as partial rather than fully mature.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: G2P digital payments are in active use across multiple programs. Government employee salaries are paid via e-zwich/digital channels — the e-zwich system has been used to filter all civil servant payroll since at least 2015, eliminating ghost workers (35,000 ghost workers eliminated saving $35M/year in one department). The LEAP social protection program (99th cycle as of Dec 2025, 350,580 households, GH₵139.3M disbursed per cycle) uses digital channels. During COVID-19, Ghana used digital payments for social protection cash transfers at scale. Pilot of mobile money payments for LEAP beneficiaries announced August 2025. Ghana's National Payment Systems Strategic Plan (2019-2024) set a target of at least 95% of G2P payments electronically.
revision_notes: Confirmed G2P digital payments remain in active use: LEAP cash transfers have used e-zwich/GhIPSS electronic disbursement since 2015, and since August 2025 the government has piloted a transition to GhanaPay mobile money in 50 districts. The Ghana Social Protection Act 2024 (Act 1121) provides an updated legal framework. A June 2026 academic case study confirms the hybrid digital payment system combining e-zwich and biometric verification remains operational, albeit with rural infrastructure gaps. Score of 3 (Yes - Active Use) confirmed.
revised_comments: Government-to-person digital payments are in active use. Civil service salaries and pensions are paid through electronic/bank channels, and the LEAP social protection programme has disbursed cash grants electronically via GhIPSS and e-zwich since 2015. Since August 2025 the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection has been piloting a transition of LEAP payments to GhanaPay mobile money in 50 districts, aimed at improving reach in hard-to-reach communities ahead of a possible nationwide rollout. The Ghana Social Protection Act, 2024 (Act 1121) provides the legal framework coordinating these programmes. Infrastructure and connectivity gaps persist in some remote districts.

Definition: Whether the system enables consumer payments to merchants and businesses for goods and services, including retail purchases, bill payments, e-commerce, and subscription services.
Comments: P2B payments are fully functional. GhIPSS launched GhQR (Universal QR Code) in May 2020, making Ghana the first country in Africa to harmonize QR code payments at national level, allowing payments to merchants from mobile wallets, cards, and bank accounts. Merchant payments via mobile money exceeded $100 billion globally in 2024, with Ghana as a major contributor. Ghana's National Payment Systems Strategic Plan explicitly promotes digital merchant payments and QR code adoption. POS terminals are deployed nationwide by banks and PSPs.
revision_notes: GhIPSS 2025 industry performance data confirms continued growth of merchant/wallet-based payments: MMI wallet-to-wallet transactions reached 282.95 million valued at GHS39.71 billion in 2025, and the GhanaPay mobile money platform's transaction volume rose nearly eightfold. GhQR remains part of the payment ecosystem for merchant acceptance. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed.
revised_comments: Person-to-business merchant payments are fully functional. GhIPSS launched the Universal QR Code (GhQR) in May 2020, the first national harmonised QR standard in Africa, enabling payment to merchants from mobile wallets, cards and bank accounts. Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI) processed 290.31 million transactions worth GHS51.60 billion in 2025, with wallet-to-wallet and merchant transactions the dominant use case, while the GhanaPay mobile money platform grew nearly eightfold in transaction volume during the year. POS terminals are deployed nationwide by banks and payment service providers.

Definition: Whether the system enables citizen payments to government for taxes, fees, licenses, fines, utility bills, and other government service charges.
Comments: P2G digital payments are in active use. The GRA (Ghana Revenue Authority) Taxpayers' Portal and App were officially launched April 2022, allowing all taxpayers to file returns and make payments online via mobile money, bank card, USSD *222# or bank visit. Tax clearance certificates can only be generated via the portal. Ghana.gov is the government digital payment platform. The E-levy (introduced May 2022, repealed 2025) collected GH₵810.5M in H1 2024, demonstrating widespread digital payment use for government levies. P2G payments include school/hospital fees, utility bills, and NHIS premiums via mobile money. The Digital Financial Services Policy (2020) explicitly targets digitization of P2G payments.
revision_notes: GRA Taxpayers' Portal confirmed still operational in 2026 for P2G tax payments (mobile money, bank card, USSD). E-levy itself was repealed April 2025, removing one P2G revenue stream, but other digital P2G payment mechanisms (tax filing/payment, NHIS premiums, utility bills via mobile money) remain active and the GRA reports continued strong digital revenue collection into 2026. Score of 3 (Yes - Active Use) confirmed, updated to reflect the E-levy repeal.
revised_comments: Citizen-to-government digital payments are in active use. The GRA Taxpayers' Portal and mobile app, launched April 2022, allow taxpayers to file returns and pay taxes via mobile money, bank card, USSD *222# or at a bank; tax clearance certificates are issued only through the portal. Ghana.gov is the central government digital payment platform, and NHIS premiums, school and hospital fees, and utility bills are commonly paid via mobile money. The Electronic Transfer Levy (E-levy), introduced in 2022, was repealed in April 2025, but the government reports that other digital revenue channels have more than offset the change, with GRA collecting GHS33.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026, 20% up year-on-year.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports direct person-to-person transfer of funds between individuals for informal transactions, remittances, and interpersonal value transfers.
Comments: P2P payments are fully functional and dominant. GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP) enables real-time interbank P2P transfers. Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI, launched May 2018) enables cross-network wallet-to-wallet (W2W) transfers as the dominant use case — accounting for 83% of total MMI transaction value in 2023. E-zwich also supports P2P. By 2023, mobile money recorded 6.81 billion transactions valued at GH₵1.92 trillion. MTN MoMo, Vodafone Cash, and AirtelTigo Money serve over 65 million accounts.
revision_notes: 2025/2026 Bank of Ghana and GhIPSS data confirm P2P transfers remain the dominant use case: interoperable mobile money transaction value rose from GHS3.1bn (December 2024) to GHS5.8bn (December 2025), an 87% increase, with wallet-to-wallet transfers accounting for 282.95 million of MMI's 290.31 million transactions in 2025. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed with updated figures.
revised_comments: Person-to-person payments are fully functional and remain the dominant use case on Ghana's interoperable payment rails. GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP) supports real-time interbank P2P transfers, while Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI), launched in 2018, enables wallet-to-wallet transfers across networks; these accounted for 282.95 million of MMI's 290.31 million transactions in 2025, valued at GHS39.71 billion. Bank of Ghana data show the value of interoperable mobile money transactions grew 87% year-on-year to GHS5.8 billion in December 2025. E-zwich also supports P2P transfers.

Definition: Whether and how the central bank participates in payment system governance beyond its regulatory oversight role, including board representation, operational management, technical standard-setting, or direct system operation.
Comments: The Bank of Ghana directly operates digital payment infrastructure through GhIPSS, its wholly owned subsidiary. GhIPSS was established in May 2007 by the Bank of Ghana with the mandate to implement and manage interoperable payment system infrastructures. The Bank of Ghana also licenses all payment service providers, sets rules, issues guidelines (including ISO 20022 messaging, Disclosure and Transparency Guidelines), oversees the RTGS/GIS system directly, and chairs the Payment Systems Advisory Committee. The Bank has direct operational control, not merely regulatory oversight.
revision_notes: Re-confirmed via the GhIPSS 'About' page and the Bank of Ghana 2024 Annual Report: GhIPSS remains a wholly owned subsidiary of the Bank of Ghana, established 2007, with the Bank of Ghana directly operating national payment infrastructure (GIP, MMI, e-zwich, gh-link, GACH) alongside its regulatory role of licensing PSPs and issuing scheme guidelines. Score of 5 (Direct Operation) confirmed; this is a structural fact unlikely to have changed and is corroborated by two independent official sources.
revised_comments: The Bank of Ghana directly operates the country's core digital payment infrastructure through GhIPSS, its wholly owned subsidiary established in 2007 to implement and manage interoperable payment systems, including GhIPSS Instant Pay, Mobile Money Interoperability, e-zwich and the national switch. Beyond this direct operational role, the Bank of Ghana also licenses and regulates all payment service providers, sets technical and messaging standards (including ISO 20022), and chairs the Payment Systems Advisory Committee.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Ghana has comprehensive consumer protection provisions for digital payments. The Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) contains dedicated consumer protection provisions (Section 44: Principles of consumer protection; Section 45: Responsibilities of PSPs; Section 46: Rights and responsibilities of electronic money holder; Section 47: Complaint procedure requiring all PSPs to establish internal dispute resolution). The Bank of Ghana enforces these and adjudicates unresolved complaints within 20 days. The Bank also issued a Disclosure and Transparency Guidelines Exposure Draft (2022) with detailed consumer disclosure requirements. The Consumer Recourse Mechanism Guidelines for Financial Service Providers also apply to GhIPSS participants.
revision_notes: Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) consumer protection provisions (sections 44-47) remain in force with no repeal identified. The Bank of Ghana continues to enforce complaint resolution timelines. Score of 3 (Yes) confirmed; no material change found.
revised_comments: Ghana has comprehensive consumer protection provisions specific to digital payments. The Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) contains dedicated consumer protection sections: Section 44 sets out principles of consumer protection, Section 45 the responsibilities of payment service providers, Section 46 the rights of electronic money holders, and Section 47 requires all PSPs to establish internal dispute resolution mechanisms, with unresolved complaints escalated to the Bank of Ghana for adjudication within 20 days. The Bank of Ghana's Disclosure and Transparency Guidelines for Digital Financial Services add further consumer disclosure requirements.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Data breach notification is mandatory under Ghana's Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843). Where there are reasonable grounds to believe personal data has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person, the data controller must notify the Data Protection Commission and the data subject 'as soon as reasonably practicable' after discovery. A LinkedIn compliance guide cites a 72-hour notification requirement to the DPC. The Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) Section 34 also requires PSPs to make quick reports to the Bank of Ghana if systems go down or are compromised. Notification may be delayed only if security agencies or the DPC determine it would impede a criminal investigation.
revision_notes: Confirmed mandatory data breach notification remains in force under the Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843, notify DPC/data subject 'as soon as reasonably practicable') and the Cybersecurity Act 2020 (Act 1038, 24-hour incident reporting for licensed CII providers/financial institutions). A new Data Protection Bill 2025 (published for consultation November 2025, not yet enacted) would formalise a 72-hour notification deadline with administrative penalties. Score of 3 (Mandatory) confirmed and updated with 2025 evidence of further strengthening in train.
revised_comments: Data breach notification is mandatory in Ghana. The Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) requires data controllers to notify the Data Protection Commission and affected data subjects as soon as reasonably practicable after discovering unauthorised access to personal data. The Cybersecurity Act 2020 (Act 1038) separately requires licensed critical information infrastructure providers, including financial institutions, to report cybersecurity incidents within 24 hours, and the Bank of Ghana requires financial institutions to report data breaches immediately with monthly incident summaries. A draft Data Protection Bill 2025, under public consultation since late 2025, would formalise a 72-hour breach notification deadline with administrative penalties for non-compliance.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Ghana has both general data protection legislation and specific payment data provisions. The Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) is the primary data protection law, requiring data controllers to register, obtain consent, and notify the DPC and data subjects of breaches. Additionally, the Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) contains specific payment data provisions including Section 34 (data security, fraud monitoring, 6-year audit log retention, mandatory incident reporting to Bank of Ghana), and the Bank of Ghana's Disclosure and Transparency Guidelines for Digital Financial Services (2022 Exposure Draft) impose specific rules on PSPs regarding consumer data collection and sharing. The Cybersecurity Act 2020 (Act 1038) adds further provisions.
revision_notes: Confirmed the Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) Section 34 payment-specific data security/retention provisions remain in force, reinforced by a 2025 Bank of Ghana requirement for PSPs/DEMIs to upgrade to ISO 27001:2022 certification by 31 October 2025. The general Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) remains the overarching framework. Score of 3 (Specific Payment Data Provisions) confirmed.
revised_comments: Ghana's data protection framework explicitly covers payment transaction data. The general Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) requires data controllers to register, obtain consent and secure personal data, while the Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987), Section 34, imposes payment-specific requirements including fraud monitoring, a six-year audit log retention period and mandatory incident reporting to the Bank of Ghana. The Bank of Ghana has also directed payment service providers and dedicated electronic money issuers to upgrade to ISO 27001:2022 certification by 31 October 2025, and the Cybersecurity Act 2020 (Act 1038) adds further security obligations.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Pro-poor governance is explicitly embedded in GhIPSS mandate and Bank of Ghana policy. The e-zwich system was specifically designed to serve unbanked, under-banked and banked segments. Ghana's National Payment Systems Strategic Plan (2019-2024) and Digital Financial Services Policy (2020) explicitly prioritize financial inclusion. The LEAP social protection cash transfer program (350,580 households as of Dec 2025) is being migrated to mobile money payments. GhIPSS' mandate explicitly includes delivery to unbanked populations. Bank of Ghana Financial Inclusion for Persons with Disabilities Directive (Exposure Draft, October 2024) mandates all FSPs to accommodate persons with disabilities. NFIDS (National Financial Inclusion Development Strategy) also guides inclusive policy.
revision_notes: Pro-poor governance mechanisms confirmed and expanded: the Ghana Social Protection Act 2024 (Act 1121) establishes a coordinating legal framework, and the 2025 LEAP mobile money pilot (50 districts) explicitly targets accessibility for hard-to-reach and vulnerable beneficiaries at no transaction cost. GhanaPay is providing on-site training to beneficiaries. Score of 3 (Yes) confirmed with fresher evidence.
revised_comments: Pro-poor governance is explicitly embedded in Ghana's payment system institutions and social protection policy. GhIPSS' e-zwich platform was designed to serve unbanked and under-banked segments, and the Ghana Social Protection Act 2024 (Act 1121) provides a coordinating legal framework for social protection programmes. Since August 2025 the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection has piloted free GhanaPay mobile money payments for LEAP beneficiaries across 50 districts, explicitly aimed at reaching households in hard-to-reach communities, supported by on-site training on account use and safeguarding. The Bank of Ghana's Financial Inclusion for Persons with Disabilities Directive further mandates accommodations across financial service providers.

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: GhIPSS scheme rules are described as partially public. Technical documentation references adherence to legislation and regulation, and the GhIPSS website publishes general information about its systems and mandates. However, detailed scheme rules for GIP, MMI, and other systems are not fully publicly available — they are referenced in research case studies as available only through stakeholder interviews or upon request. The Bank of Ghana publishes its Payment Systems Oversight Annual Reports (annual), regulatory guidelines, and exposure drafts openly, but comprehensive scheme rulebooks are not fully on the public website. Scheme rules requiring participants to adhere to 24/7 uptime, consumer recourse mechanisms etc. are referenced in research but not posted in full publicly.
revision_notes: The GhIPSS website and the Bank of Ghana Payment Systems Downloads page continue to publish general system information, guidelines and annual oversight reports, but no full public scheme rulebook for GIP/MMI was located in 2025-2026 searches. Score of 2 (Partial - On Request) confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: GhIPSS scheme rules are only partially public. The GhIPSS and Bank of Ghana websites publish general information on system mandates, regulatory guidelines and disclosure/transparency requirements, and the Bank of Ghana's Payment Systems Downloads page hosts annual Payment Systems Oversight reports and exposure drafts. However, comprehensive scheme rulebooks setting out detailed participation, pricing and technical requirements for GIP, MMI and related systems are not published in full online and appear to be available mainly to participants or on request.

Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing an instant/real-time payment system (IPS/RTP) that enables digital payments with near-instant settlement (typically within seconds), available 24/7/365. This includes both bank-led and mobile money interoperability systems.
Comments: Ghana has a fully deployed nationwide digital payment system. GhIPSS (wholly owned subsidiary of Bank of Ghana, incorporated 2007) operates: GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP, launched 2015), Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI, launched 2018), e-zwich biometric national payment system, gh-link national switch, Ghana Automated Clearing House (GACH), Cheque Codeline Clearing (CCC), and GhQR universal QR code (launched 2020, first in Africa). All banks in Ghana participate. By 2023, total mobile money transaction value reached GH₵1.92 trillion (6.81 billion transactions). Ghana ranked #1 globally for mobile money regulation (GSMA 2024 index, score 95.06%).
revision_notes: 2025 GhIPSS industry performance data (530 million transactions, GHS1.73 trillion, +50% year-on-year) and a Bank of Ghana February 2026 statement confirm the instant payment ecosystem (GIP, MMI, e-zwich, GhQR, GACH) remains fully deployed and growing nationwide, with all banks participating. Score of 5 (Fully deployed nationwide) confirmed with fresher figures.
revised_comments: Ghana has a fully deployed, nationwide instant/real-time digital payment system. GhIPSS, the Bank of Ghana's wholly owned payment systems operator, runs GhIPSS Instant Pay (GIP, since 2015), Mobile Money Interoperability (MMI, since 2018), the e-zwich biometric national payment system, the gh-link national switch, the Ghana Automated Clearing House, and the GhQR universal QR code (the first harmonised national QR standard in Africa). All banks participate, and in 2025 GhIPSS processed 530 million transactions worth GHS1.73 trillion, a 50% increase in value on 2024, with mobile money interoperability transaction value up 87% year-on-year by December 2025.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: Active digital payment users are estimated at 50-69% of adults. Ghana had 68% of adults with any financial account (bank or mobile money) as of December 2021 (Findex 2021). By late 2023, mobile money accounts surpassed 65 million (Ghana population ~33M adults, suggesting significant multi-account holders). Ghana achieved approximately 96% financial service access (including all forms) by 2024, surpassing its 85% national target. However, 'active users' of digital payments specifically — those making/receiving digital payments — is somewhat lower than account ownership. The unbanked fell from ~60% in 2014 to 32% in 2021. Given 68% account ownership in 2021 and continued growth, digital payment active users are in the 50-69% range for adults.
revision_notes: The World Bank Global Findex 2025 (2024 survey data) reports Ghana's mobile money account ownership at 75.7% of adults (age 15+), up from approximately 68% overall account ownership (bank and mobile money combined) in the 2021 Findex round. This, combined with GhIPSS 2025 transaction data showing 530 million transactions across GIP/MMI/GhanaPay, indicates usage is now well above the previous 50-69% band. Account ownership is a proxy rather than a direct measure of transactions in the past 90 days, so this recalculation is made with medium confidence. Recalculated from 3 (50-69%) to 4 (70-89%).
revised_comments: Active use of digital payments is estimated in the 70-89% range of the adult population. The World Bank's Global Findex 2025 (based on 2024 survey data) records mobile money account ownership in Ghana at 75.7% of adults aged 15 and above, up from around 68% total account ownership (bank and mobile money combined) in the 2021 round. GhIPSS reported 530 million transactions across its instant payment platforms in 2025, a 32% increase in volume on 2024, consistent with high levels of active use. Precise 90-day active-user data are not separately published, so this estimate relies on account ownership and transaction volume as proxies.

Definition: Whether independent external audits of payment system security, operations, financial controls, and compliance are conducted by third-party auditors, and whether audit results or summaries are made public.
Comments: Public audits and reviews are conducted. GhIPSS holds PCI DSS certification and ISO 27001 certification (both publicly disclosed on ghipss.net). In 2023, the Bank of Ghana conducted a self-assessment of the RTGS system against the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI) — the first such assessment in Ghana — and the outcome was publicly reported as 'broadly compliant' in the 2023 Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report. The Bank of Ghana's annual Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report is publicly available and provides a comprehensive review of the payment ecosystem. The assessment of systemically important payment systems against PFMI is an internationally recognized public audit standard.
revision_notes: Bank of Ghana Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report 2024 confirmed published (bog.gov.gh), continuing the practice of public annual reporting alongside GhIPSS's PCI DSS and ISO 27001 certifications. Score of 3 (Public Audits) confirmed with the 2024 report as the freshest evidence.
revised_comments: Independent audits and reviews of Ghana's payment systems are conducted and publicly reported. Definition: Percentage of government payments (G2P disbursements including salaries, pensions, social transfers) made through instant digital payment system rather than cash or check, reflecting government adoption and modernization.
Comments: Government adoption of digital payments for government-related transactions is in the 50-69% range. Ghana's National Payment Systems Strategic Plan (2019-2024) set a target of 95% of G2P payments being electronic, and the government has made significant progress. Civil servant salaries are digitally paid via e-zwich and bank accounts. LEAP (350,580 households) pays digitally. Tax collection via GRA portal is active. However, full adoption across all government departments and all payment flows (including rural social protection, informal sector pensions, P2G payments) has not yet reached 70%+ given ongoing gaps in rural areas and partial LEAP mobile money migration. The Digital Financial Services Policy (2020) acknowledges remaining gaps.
revision_notes: LEAP mobile money migration remains at pilot stage (50 districts as of August 2025) rather than nationwide, and a June 2026 academic case study confirms continuing infrastructure and access gaps in remote districts for LEAP payment delivery. Score of 3 (50-69%) confirmed as no authoritative percentage figure above this range was found.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: Refugee and migrant access to digital payments is partial. Foreigners can register for SIM cards and mobile money in Ghana using a passport (for short stays up to 90 days) or a non-citizen Ghana Card (for stays over 90 days). The non-citizen Ghana Card is available to all residents and costs approximately $120. With a non-citizen card, users can register up to 10 SIM cards and access mobile money. However, registration requirements (requiring either a Ghana Card PIN or non-citizen card) create barriers for refugees and informal migrants who may lack documentation. A 2026 SIM re-registration exercise requires biometric verification against the NIA database, which may further restrict access for undocumented migrants. UNHCR-registered refugees with documentation can in principle access services, but informal/undocumented migrants face significant barriers.
revision_notes: The 2026 NCA SIM Re-Registration FAQs confirm a formal, named pathway for refugees (a 'Refugee Non-Citizen ID') alongside categories for foreign residents, visitors and diplomats, an improvement in documentation clarity over the earlier 2022 evidence, which relied on informal reporting (Reddit, Yen.com.gh). However, all registrants, including refugees, must undergo real-time biometric verification against the NIA database, which continues to create a practical barrier for undocumented or informally settled refugees/migrants lacking recognised ID. Score of 2 (Partial) confirmed with clearer, more authoritative 2026 evidence of the access pathway and its limits.
revised_comments: Refugee and migrant access to digital payment accounts in Ghana is partial. Ghana's 2026 SIM (Number) Registration framework formally recognises refugees as an eligible category, requiring a Refugee Non-Citizen ID, alongside separate pathways for foreign residents (Non-Citizen Ghana Card), visitors (passport plus proof of entry) and diplomats. Registration and SIM activation, a practical prerequisite for mobile money access, require real-time biometric verification against the National Identification Authority database. This creates a formal legal pathway for documented refugees but continues to exclude undocumented or informally settled migrants who lack recognised identification, and non-compliant lines are subject to automatic deactivation.
